cells.tense: The letting go is happening with you, not to you, and it's happening now.
cells.ask: Feed what's growing here instead: give the next thing one small act of care today, nothing forced behind it, and let it answer in its own time.
cells.core:
When this is going well, an ending gets to be an ending. Something finishes, and you can tell it finished, so you set it down without a fight. It's not collapse and it's not losing — it's release that follows from the thing being done. What you've cleared, you've cleared on purpose, and you're standing in the open space you made.

That's what makes the next part possible. The quiet isn't a wound to fill; it's ground. Let some care land in it — one small tending, no force behind it — and what's growing answers on its own clock. You don't have to pull it up to check that it took.
cells.sheetLine: You're setting it down on purpose, and what you cleared gives the next thing room.
cells.verb: letting go on purpose, clearing space by releasing your grip
cells.place: where what has ended has to fully end for what's next to come through

cells.tense: You're bracing for an ending that hasn't arrived, and living in advance of it.
cells.ask: Keep one small steady practice going on what's still here — a little attention, repeated — instead of rehearsing the goodbye.
cells.core:
When this is going well, endings get their full length. Nothing is abandoned before it's finished and nothing is carried past its time. Things are allowed to complete, and the completing is what lets the next thing in.

What's bending this now is speed. You're letting go before the thing is finished — dropping it early, folding before you're asked to, making the leaving louder than it needed to be. The endings still happen; they just happen ahead of their time. Discipline is the way through here, not in the sense of grinding — a small steady practice, kept quietly, on what's actually still in front of you. Stay with one thing long enough to find out whether it's done, and let the ending come when it comes.
cells.sheetLine: You're letting go before anything's finished, and the endings come out louder than they need to.
cells.verb: letting go on purpose, clearing space by releasing your grip
cells.place: where what has ended has to fully end for what's next to come through

cells.tense: The thing ended a way back, and you're still standing where you stopped.
cells.ask: Hold one thing steadily — a form that carries weight without tightening — and let that give you something solid to stand on.
cells.core:
When this is going well, you can set things down. A job outgrows you, a version of yourself is finished, someone leaves the picture — and it's released as a completion. That's the natural motion here, and the room it leaves is the point.

What's happening now is that nothing has been set down. Keep a hold on something long past its use and the arm doesn't rest — it gets tired. There's a kind of holding left in you, but it's endurance, not grip: the ability to bear weight and stay shaped while you do. Let one thing stay exactly as it is, and find out you can carry it without clenching. That's how the opening gets made.
cells.sheetLine: You're still holding what's already over, and the holding is what's wearing you down.
cells.verb: letting go on purpose, clearing space by releasing your grip
cells.place: where what has ended has to fully end for what's next to come through

cells.tense: The letting go is already under way, and you're talking about it like it's something you're still deciding.
cells.ask: Tend the small thing that's still alive here — a day's care, nothing forced — and let that show what you're actually keeping.
cells.core:
When this works, it works by making room. What's finished gets released, the grip loosens, and something underneath the grasping gets to show itself. You feel the release land and you know what it was for.

Right now it's running without your say-so. Either something already ended and you're still calling it ongoing, or something ended for you and you're calling it a plan you made. Care is the way back in: not a rescue, just keeping one small living thing tended — a plant, a routine, a person — and letting what you're actually holding onto come clear from that.
cells.sheetLine: The release is already happening. You're the last one to say so.
